title: Can Technology Facilitate Scale? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation of High Dosage Tutoring
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether technology can help scale high-dosage tutoring without substantially reducing its effectiveness. The core problem is that high-dosage tutoring has strong evidence of improving student learning, but large-scale implementation is constrained by cost and tutor staffing. The study asks whether substituting part of tutor time with computer-assisted learning (CAL) can preserve learning gains while lowering per-student costs and labor requirements.

The intervention studied is a hybrid math tutoring model developed by Saga Education. In this 4-to-1 model, four 9th-grade students met with one in-person tutor during a daily 50-minute class period. On a given day, two students worked directly with the tutor while the other two used the ALEKS adaptive computer-assisted learning platform; students alternated roles across days. This model was designed to reduce costs relative to Saga’s prior 2-to-1 daily tutoring model while maintaining individualized support and structured instruction.

The study was a student-level randomized controlled trial involving about 4,000 students across seven public high schools in two large U.S. school districts: Chicago Public Schools and New York City Public Schools, spanning the 2018-19 and 2019-20 school years. The primary analysis focuses on the 2018-19 cohort because COVID-19 disrupted end-of-year testing in 2019-20. Students were primarily first-time 9th graders eligible for participation based on scheduling and prior attendance/academic criteria. Outcomes were drawn from administrative records, including standardized math test scores, grades, course failures, attendance, and suspensions.

The main conclusion is that the hybrid tutoring-plus-technology model produced substantial positive effects on math achievement. For the first cohort, the treatment-on-the-treated effect on standardized math test scores was 0.23 standard deviations, with positive effects also found on math GPA and math course failures. These gains were nearly as large as those from the more expensive 2-to-1 daily tutoring model, while reducing per-pupil costs by about 30 percent and halving tutor staffing needs. The study suggests that strategic use of adaptive learning technology can support the scalability of high-dosage tutoring, though effects were concentrated in math and not evident for broader behavioral or non-math outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ALEKS
identified_tools.description: ALEKS is an adaptive online mathematics learning platform that assesses students' current knowledge and personalizes instructional content and practice problems accordingly.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the computer-assisted learning component within Saga Education's in-school 4-to-1 9th-grade math tutoring model. In treatment, groups of four alternated between tutor-led work and class periods on ALEKS; the comparison condition was business-as-usual instruction and services.

findings.finding_summary: In cohort 1 (AY2018-19), the Saga Technology tutoring model that incorporated ALEKS improved end-of-year standardized math test scores. Reported effects were 0.19 SD intent-to-treat and 0.23 SD treatment-on-the-treated in the randomized sample.
In cohort 1 (AY2018-19), the Saga Technology tutoring model that incorporated ALEKS increased math course GPA by 0.24 grade points.
In cohort 1 (AY2018-19), the Saga Technology tutoring model that incorporated ALEKS reduced math course failures by 22%.
In cohort 1, the paper reports no detectable effects of the Saga Technology tutoring model that incorporated ALEKS on non-math academic outcomes.
In cohort 1, the paper reports no detectable effects of the Saga Technology tutoring model that incorporated ALEKS on behavioral outcomes such as attendance and suspensions.
For cohort 2 (AY2019-20), pre-disruption outcomes were qualitatively similar: the treatment-on-the-treated effect on mid-year math GPA was 0.21 grade points.
For cohort 2 (AY2019-20), the treatment-on-the-treated effect on mid-year math course failures was -0.05, qualitatively similar to cohort 1.

For cohort 1 follow-up in the subsequent school year, the Saga Technology tutoring model that incorporated ALEKS showed a positive treatment-on-the-treated effect of 0.15 grade points on mid-year math GPA.

For cohort 1 follow-up in the subsequent school year, the paper reports a 20% reduction in first-semester math course failures for students previously offered the Saga Technology tutoring model that incorporated ALEKS.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a large student-level randomized controlled trial with administrative outcome data and a control group, but there are some concerns including baseline imbalance, principal discretion in assignment implementation in NYC, and the paper being an NBER working paper that had not yet been peer reviewed.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported treatment-on-the-treated effect on standardized math achievement was 0.23 SD, exceeding the 0.20 threshold for a strong impact tier, with additional positive effects on math GPA and math course failures.
